clue.text: I don't expect change from my tuppenny-ha'penny

definitions.text: I don't expect change from my tuppenny-ha'penny

parts.words: I don't expect change from my tuppenny-ha'penny
parts.note: offering a modest opinion, a 'two pennies' worth', the speaker admits it may change nothing, rather than asking for coins back

explanation.surface: A shopper hands over a tiny old-fashioned sum and waives the change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like coins returned, but it means a change of mind or situation. Tuppenny-ha'penny (two and a half old pence) is British slang for something trifling, here a small contribution to a discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom offering a remark modestly, with no expectation that it will alter anyone's view.

clue.text: This, turning into thoroughfare? Oh, no!

indicators.note: turning means twisting the remaining letters into a new order
'Oh, no!' says the letters of oh are not wanted, so they are removed

explanation.surface: A driver, changing up as they turn onto a main road, exclaims in dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: Semi-&lit: 'This' is the definition and the whole clue pictures the gear. Remove OH from THOROUGHFARE and 'turning' rearranges what remains, TRUGHFARE.
explanation.definitionFit: On a main road you would shift up into a higher cog, so 'this' points at the gear the scene describes.

clue.text: Walls of address lost proportion

indicators.note: walls are the outside, so the first and last letters are meant
lost means those outer letters are taken away

parts.note: an oration is a formal address or speech

explanation.surface: A speech that has lost its framing loses all sense of proportion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walls of' and 'lost' together strip the outer O and N from ORATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio expresses the relative size of two quantities, a synonym for proportion.

clue.text: King portrayed in memorial phoney? That must be wrong — Charlemagne ruled it first

indicators.note: something that must be wrong needs putting right, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A fake memorial shows a king, and Charlemagne was the first to rule.
explanation.walkthrough: R (rex) and MEMORIAL PHONEY are rearranged, signalled by 'must be wrong'; 'portrayed in' only joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlemagne, crowned in 800, is regarded as the first emperor of that central European realm.

clue.text: Tam or Pat's early salutation?

parts.note: the first letter (top) of 'the' is T, and 'of the morning' is AM, making these three letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Scot or an Irishman gives this greeting at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Tam and Pat look like two men. Pat is the stock Irishman; this phrase is a stereotypical Irish good-morning.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a traditional Irish greeting used early in the day to wish someone well.

clue.text: Where Nijinsky was driven round the bend

definitions.text: Where Nijinsky was driven round the bend

parts.words: Where Nijinsky was driven round the bend
parts.note: not the dancer going mad but the racehorse, Derby winner of 1970, ridden round the famous bend at Epsom

explanation.surface: The ballet dancer Nijinsky, who suffered mental illness, was driven mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Nijinsky was also a racehorse who won the 1970 Derby at Epsom Downs, which has a famous downhill bend.
explanation.definitionFit: That bend is the sharp turn into the home straight on Epsom's Derby course.

clue.text: Met objective expending only a third of energy, so we'll take a group of players round

indicators.note: take, with round, means holding something inside
round means the outer letters go round the inner ones

parts.note: the clue's 'we' gives WE
a cast is the group of actors in a play

indicators.note: the word for so has three of the energy letter, and one of them is spent

parts.note: therefore means so, as a consequence
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A goal pursued with little effort, while a band plays around us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met' is the Met Office, Britain's weather service. The word for 'so' has three Es, and 'expending only a third of' spends just one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Predicting tomorrow's conditions is the core purpose of the national meteorological service.

clue.text: Put new structure on back burner

parts.note: the rear is the back
a range is a cooking stove with burners

explanation.surface: An instruction to shelve a project on the back burner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back burner' reads as a single idiom for postponing, but the two words work separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To rearrange is to reorganise, putting things into a different order or layout.

clue.text: Tilt knob

definitions.meaning: a ship leans over to one side
British slang for a contemptible man, a cad

explanation.surface: A knob on a machine that tilts something.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that tilts is said to heel over; a knob, in British slang, is a cad or rotter.

clue.text: Attribute of great-aunt I look up to

indicators.note: something that is an attribute of these words belongs to them, so the letters sit inside the run of words

explanation.surface: A child admires a quality of an elderly relative they look up to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up to' reads as part of 'look up to', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are prepositions of time meaning as far as a stated point, as in 'wait up to noon'.

clue.text: Apt, the garbage consuming Henry Salt!

indicators.note: the jumbled letters eat up the name, holding it inside them
garbage is jumbled rubbish, so the letters of these words are muddled

parts.note: Hal is a familiar short form of Henry, as with Prince Hal

explanation.surface: An exclamation that some rubbish has swallowed a man called Henry Salt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consuming' puts HAL inside PHTATE, the anagram of APT THE from 'garbage'. 'Henry Salt' looks like one person's name, but the surname is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemists class this compound, used to make plastics softer, as a salt or ester of phthalic acid.

clue.text: For couple over in Yorkshire, anything goes

indicators.note: turned over, so the letters of the dialect word are read backwards

parts.note: owt is the northern English, especially Yorkshire, dialect word for anything

explanation.surface: In Yorkshire, anything goes for a married couple.
explanation.walkthrough: OWT (Yorkshire dialect for 'anything', as in 'owt or nowt') is read backwards, signalled by 'over'.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple is a pair of things, and a pair numbers precisely that many.

clue.text: Take charge of race, overlooking superb setting of Sandown Park's courses

parts.note: to referee a match is to take charge of it; ref is the short form

indicators.note: overlooking means leaving out, so a word for superb is removed from race

parts.note: ace means excellent or superb
Esher in Surrey is the town where Sandown Park racecourse stands, so this is Esher's

explanation.surface: A steward takes over a race meeting at the splendid Sandown Park courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' removes ACE from RACE, leaving R. SANDOWN PARK is a racecourse in Esher, Surrey; 'courses' looks like racecourses but means training courses.
explanation.definitionFit: Refreshers are short training courses that update earlier learning, as in a refresher course.

clue.text: Time woman's managed to divide gives go-ahead to soldiers

indicators.note: to divide means splitting the outer word in two with the others

parts.note: OKs means approves or gives the go-ahead
her is the possessive for a woman
ran means managed, as in ran a business

explanation.surface: A woman's management splits the time before soldiers get the green light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to divide' splits OKs (approves) around the time, woman and managed pieces; 'go-ahead' is the verb's object, not a noun alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase covers army personnel who are not commissioned officers, the rank and file.

clue.text: Bound so excitedly, a bulge appearing in middle of tights

indicators.note: appearing in means showing up inside, so these letters go within the others
the middle of a six-letter word is its central pair of letters

parts.note: a lump is a swelling or bulge

explanation.surface: A dancer leaps exuberantly, and an unflattering bulge shows in the tights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like tied up, but with 'so excitedly' it describes leaping; 'middle of' takes the central pair of the six-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: To galumph is to move in a clumsy, exuberant, bounding way, a word coined by Lewis Carroll.

clue.text: Seducers blowing hot air in the Rising Sun

indicators.note: the jumbled hot air is placed in the reversed sun, so in here means held inside it
in a down entry rising means read from the bottom up

parts.note: Sol is the Latin name for the sun

indicators.note: blowing scatters the letters like wind

explanation.surface: Seducers spout empty talk at a pub called the Rising Sun.
explanation.walkthrough: SOL rises to LOS; 'blowing' gives OTHARI, an anagram of HOT AIR. Lothario is the rake in Rowe's The Fair Penitent.
explanation.definitionFit: A lothario is a womaniser, after the libertine of an eighteenth-century play.

clue.text: Tough, hot and windy plain?

parts.note: H stands for hot, as on a tap

indicators.note: winding back on itself, so the word for the plain is turned round

parts.note: tundra is the vast treeless Arctic plain

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a plain can be tough, hot and windy all at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'windy' looks like a description of the plain, but in its sense of winding it signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough, as a noun, is a hard man or bruiser, and a hard nut is just such a person.

clue.text: Letter read out by customer in taverna?

indicators.note: read out means said aloud, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: a customer in a taverna, a Greek restaurant, is an eater

explanation.surface: A waiter reads a letter aloud to a diner in a Greek restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The taverna sets up Greek; in a non-rhotic British accent 'eater' sounds like eta.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the seventh character of the Greek alphabet, written like a long-tailed n.

clue.text: An award for theatrical excellence given to Mark? Nick's could be free

parts.note: the Tony is the Broadway award for theatre
M is the abbreviation for mark, an old German currency

explanation.surface: An actor called Mark wins a Tony, while someone called Nick goes free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name but is the verb meaning arrest, whose opposite is to free.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of opposite meaning: the opposite of nick, to arrest, could be to set free.

clue.text: Who in the end divides bread and last of the fish?

indicators.note: divides means splitting the word for bread into two

parts.note: bread is slang for money

indicators.note: the end of this word is its final letter
the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A riddle asking who ends up sharing out bread and the last of the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the loaves and fishes; 'bread' is slang for MONEY.
explanation.definitionFit: The mooneye is a North American freshwater species with large eyes, related to the goldeye.

clue.text: To impress fan calls the London Stadium this now?

definitions.meaning: to drive a point forcefully, impressing it on someone

definitions.text: fan calls the London Stadium this now?
definitions.meaning: West Ham United, nicknamed the Hammers, moved to the London Stadium, so a fan calls it the Hammers' home

explanation.surface: A football supporter's name for the London Stadium is meant to impress.
explanation.walkthrough: West Ham United, a London football club nicknamed the Hammers, moved to the London Stadium (the 2012 Olympic stadium) in 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive an argument repeatedly and forcefully until it sinks in is to impress it on the listener.

clue.text: Musical appreciation of grime artiste?

indicators.note: of means taken from within, so the letters come out of this pair of words

explanation.surface: A query about whether a grime performer has a musical gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Grime is a British style of rap music.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a good ear means having the ability to perceive and appreciate music and pitch.

clue.text: Composer worked up left extremely angry?

indicators.note: in a down entry, worked up means read from the bottom to the top
the letters for angry sit at both extremes, either side of left

parts.note: rage is extreme anger, standing for angry

explanation.surface: A question whether a composer was worked up and left really cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked up' looks like agitated, but in a down clue it reads RAGLE (RAGE round L, signalled by 'extremely') bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward Elgar wrote the Enigma Variations and Pomp and Circumstance marches.

clue.text: Do computers up

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read bottom to top

parts.note: Macs are Apple computers

explanation.surface: An instruction to set computers up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the noun meaning a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A do, in British slang, is a swindle or con, the same as a fraud.

clue.text: Popular old industrial chemists taken in by family doctor

indicators.note: taken in by means held within, so these letters go inside the word for family

parts.note: a clan is an extended family
in means fashionable or popular
ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, the former British chemicals giant

explanation.surface: A GP is fooled by some well-liked former industrial chemists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'family doctor' reads as a GP, but 'family' is CLAN and only 'doctor' defines. ICI was a major British chemicals company, broken up in 2008.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinician is a medical practitioner who treats patients directly, as a doctor does.

clue.text: Deficient in iron, ready to drop another element

indicators.note: deficient in means lacking, so the symbol for iron is taken out

parts.note: far gone means exhausted or near collapse
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: An anaemic person, exhausted, about to drop, needs another mineral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deficient in iron' reads like anaemia but removes FE from FAR GONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, the inert noble gas used in light bulbs.

clue.text: Court official, playing games, arrests men

indicators.note: playing about with these letters rearranges them

explanation.surface: A court officer, playing games, arrests some men.
explanation.walkthrough: A MESSENGER-AT-ARMS is a Scottish court officer who serves Court of Session documents.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer of the Scottish Court of Session serves writs and enforces its decrees.
